title: Advances and Perspectives of Mexican Microscopy, Part I: Materials Science
content: The first records of published works on electron microscopy in Mexico in the field of materials science date back to the 1960s and 1970s decades [1,2]. One of the first outstanding contributions to materials science through the use of transmission electron microscopy (TEM) was focused on the high-resolution dark-field electron-microscopy of small particles [2]. In this article, irregular shapes of decahedral and icosahedral nanoparticles were demonstrated based on weak beam dark field images, a systematic application of weak beam dark field techniques to the study of metal supported catalysts, Fig. 1A and 1B. This paper captured the attention of the catalysis community interested in surface activity of nanoparticles. Among electron microscopy groups of materials science research in Mexico, one of the more traditionally developed fields has been metallurgy. In the 80s, zinc-based alloys were extensively studied and fabricated in Mexico to combine strength and corrosion resistance [3-5]. Conventional TEM methods using two-beam conditions were employed to image defects in metallic alloys and compared with simulations. Figures 1C to 1F show Burgers vector determination of dislocations formed during a thermo-mechanical treatment to induce memory effect in Cu-Zn-Al alloy with high anisotropy [3,4]. Conventional TEM techniques at relative intermediate magnification were the focus as the two examples described in Fig. 1.
